overview: Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, partly collapsing a span, as President Trump arrived in Shenzhen for the APEC summit ahead of Thursday's first three-way talks with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. In the Gulf, Iran fired at targets in Kuwait and Bahrain after US jets struck a missile site on Iran's Qeshm Island. At home, Democrat Mary Peltola won Alaska's Senate race, giving Democrats a 56-44 majority in January, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there is no evidence linking a run of tech outages at banks, airlines and government networks, and the US lost its measles elimination status after 26 years. Nvidia beat forecasts in its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation and said he won't return, lifting tech stocks ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

stories.headline: Peltola wins Alaska Senate race, giving Democrats 56 seats
stories.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the last undecided Senate race of the midterms, about two weeks after counting began. The result gives Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress meets in January.
stories.why_it_matters: With a 56-seat Senate majority and control of the House, Democrats will set the agenda in Congress from January, including which of President Trump's nominees and bills move forward.
stories.background: Alaska counts ballots slowly because many communities are remote, and it uses ranked-choice voting, so a winner needs more than half the vote after lower-ranked candidates are eliminated. Peltola, a former U.S. House member, challenged Sullivan, a two-term incumbent. The race drew attention when a second candidate named Dan Sullivan appeared on the ballot, and allegations surfaced that Democrats had helped recruit an independent as a spoiler. Democrats had already flipped eight other Senate seats in the Nov. 3 midterms.

facts.text: Peltola defeated Sen. Dan Sullivan, a two-term Republican incumbent.
Peltola won 50.1% of the vote, according to Deutsche Welle.
The win gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate.
It was the party's ninth Senate seat flipped in the midterms and the last Senate race to be called.
Peltola, who is Yup'ik, becomes the first Alaska Native U.S. senator and the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the Senate since 2015.
Axios reported that four Alaska Native strongholds delivered more than half of Peltola's statewide lead in first-choice votes.
The race was complicated by allegations that Democrats helped recruit an independent candidate as a spoiler, and a second candidate named Dan Sullivan was on the ballot.
President Trump said voters had chosen the wrong Dan Sullivan, BBC News reported.

framing.note: Puts the result in party-tally terms as the Democrats' ninth Senate flip.
Focuses on Alaska Native voters and the historic first, not the Senate math.

stories.headline: Rubio says there is no evidence the recent wave of US tech outages is linked
stories.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila there was "zero" information that recent outages at banks, airlines, Microsoft and a classified National Security Agency network are connected or caused by a hostile actor. The administration faces calls from both parties for an explanation of the failures.
stories.why_it_matters: The outages have disrupted flights, online banking and work email for millions of people, and the government's explanation shapes whether more fixes, funding or investigations follow.
stories.background: Over roughly a week, the U.S. saw a string of technology failures: a nationwide flight ground stop on Friday, a software bug at JPMorgan Chase that delayed transactions on Monday, problems with Microsoft services and, on Tuesday, an outage of a classified NSA communications network. Online theories suggested a coordinated attack. Rubio, traveling with President Trump in Asia ahead of meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, sought to calm those concerns. Republican Rep. James Comer was among lawmakers asking for answers.

facts.text: Rubio said there was "zero" information that the outages are linked or caused by a malign actor.
Speaking in Manila, Rubio said each event has an explanation that has nothing to do with a cyber criminal.
The New York Times reported that Rubio suggested a rush to patch systems whose weaknesses are being exposed by AI may explain some failures.
CBS News counted at least eight major technology outages in the U.S. in the past week.
A classified NSA communications network went offline; the agency attributed it to routine maintenance, and officials told reporters there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
JPMorgan Chase said Monday's banking disruption was caused by a software bug, not a cyberattack.
The Associated Press reported that Trump faced criticism from allies and opponents who said the White House must answer for the outages.
Rep. James Comer said he hoped the government could find answers and be transparent.

Frames the NSA outage as part of US systems "crumbling," with no mention of a cause.

stories.headline: FAA pauses router installs after ground stop as Duffy's $50 billion request meets GOP doubts
stories.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration halted installation of new routers like the one linked to Friday's nationwide ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked Congress for $50.1 billion to modernize air traffic control, but Senate Republicans questioned the cost and the lack of detail.
stories.why_it_matters: Air travelers just lived through a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop; how Congress and the FAA respond will affect the reliability of flights heading into the holiday season and how much taxpayers spend on the system.
stories.background: The FAA relies on aging communications equipment that it has been replacing for years. On Friday a router at a remote FAA site in Arkansas flooded other parts of the network with data, forcing a rare nationwide ground stop and days of disruptions. Before the outage, Duffy had sought about $30 billion for upgrades and Congress had provided $12.5 billion. He has now asked for $50.1 billion more, which needs Congress's approval.

facts.text: The FAA paused installation of new routers after Friday's nationwide ground stop, the agency confirmed.
The ground stop lasted nearly five hours.
A preliminary federal review found that a contractor for L3Harris was replacing a router at a remote FAA site when the unit began flooding other routers.
Duffy said the root cause remains unclear and that he does not apologize for shutting the airspace.
The administration formally requested $50.1 billion from Congress to modernize air traffic control and make other airport improvements.
Senate Republicans asked for an accounting of the $12.5 billion already provided.
The one-page explanation Duffy gave senators was thin on detail and included items outside air traffic control, according to The New York Times.
The request drew skepticism from lawmakers in both parties.
The FAA said airline schedules were returning to normal.

positions.claim: Federal officials said they believed a Juniper Networks router caused the data overload.
HPE, which makes Juniper routers, said the hardware worked as designed; Duffy said investigators were still weighing installer error against a faulty router.

stories.headline: Trump warns Iran after report of possible dirty-bomb plot in Washington
stories.summary: President Trump said the U.S. takes "very seriously" a CNN report, citing intelligence assessments, that Iran may be planning a dirty-bomb or chemical attack in Washington, and warned Iran of severe consequences. The White House said there are no credible threats to the homeland, and Iran denied the report.
stories.why_it_matters: The report raises questions about the safety of the capital and could feed further escalation in the nine-month U.S. war with Iran.
stories.background: The U.S. and Iran have been at war for about nine months, with ongoing strikes on each other's forces and regional mediation so far without results. CNN reported this week that U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to set off a dirty bomb, which uses ordinary explosives to scatter radioactive material, or use a chemical weapon against senior officials in Washington. Trump, who is traveling in Asia, says preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon is his main reason for the war.

facts.text: Trump said the U.S. was taking seriously the possibility of an Iranian dirty-bomb attack in Washington after being asked about a CNN report citing intelligence assessments.
Trump said Iran would pay a price "no country has ever paid" if the threat proves real.
The White House said it is monitoring potential threats but there are no credible threats to the homeland at this time.
Iran's Foreign Ministry denied the report, and a deputy foreign minister called it a "shameful lie."
Iran warned it may strike the U.S. first if it decides a wider escalation cannot be avoided, the South China Morning Post reported.
A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to spread radioactive material and is far less destructive than a nuclear weapon.

stories.headline: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years
stories.summary: The Pan American Health Organization said Tuesday that measles is again endemic in the United States after more than 12 months of continuous spread, ending the country's elimination status for the first time since 2000. Mexico and Bolivia also lost the status.
stories.why_it_matters: Measles is again circulating steadily in the U.S., raising the risk for unvaccinated children, infants and people with weak immune systems; vaccination remains the main protection.
stories.background: A country is considered to have eliminated measles when it goes at least a year without continuous spread of one chain of the virus. The U.S. reached that mark in 2000, but large outbreaks starting in 2025 kept spreading, and this year's cases are the most since 1991. PAHO, the World Health Organization's regional office for the Americas, reviewed analyses from the CDC and an independent panel before deciding. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has a history of questioning vaccines, oversees the federal response.

facts.text: PAHO determined Tuesday that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years.
PAHO's director made the final call after 12 months of continuous transmission.
The U.S. has recorded more than 5,400 cases, the worst outbreak since 1991.
Bolivia and Mexico also lost their elimination status.
PAHO based its assessment on an analysis by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts, KFF Health News reported.
Public health experts cited declining childhood vaccination rates and cuts to public health monitoring.
Johns Hopkins expert Dr. Amish Adalja said about one in five patients is hospitalized and about one in 1,000 dies.
Incoming Democratic senators and potential presidential candidates blamed Kennedy's vaccine skepticism, The New York Times reported.

Frames it as a political fight, with Democrats blaming RFK Jr.

stories.headline: White House withdraws Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the FDA
stories.summary: The White House pulled Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination as FDA commissioner a day before the Senate health committee was set to vote, after she struggled to win enough Republican support. The agency remains without a confirmed commissioner.
stories.why_it_matters: The FDA approves drugs, vaccines and food safety rules, and the fight over its leadership affects decisions on vaccines and the abortion pill.
stories.background: President Trump nominated Overton, a physician and Trump ally known for opposing abortion, to run the Food and Drug Administration. At her September hearing senators questioned her about the abortion pill mifepristone and vaccines, and committee chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy had earlier raised concerns about her management experience. Republicans hold only a one-vote majority on the Senate health committee, so a single GOP defection could block a nominee. The White House previously withdrew surgeon general nominee Casey Means in a similar situation.

stories.headline: House Democrats vote on Jeffries as speaker nominee while Schumer and Van Hollen fight over Senate post
stories.summary: House Democrats meet privately Wednesday to elect their leaders and are expected to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker, with Jeffries pushing for a tallied vote. stories.background: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms. Jeffries of New York, the current House minority leader, is in line to be the first Black speaker, but some progressives and grassroots activists have pushed for change. In the Senate, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York for majority leader. The full House elects the speaker in a floor vote in January.

stories.headline: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge, partly collapsing a span of Russia's link to Crimea
stories.summary: Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea with missiles and drones on Nov. 17, and part of the structure collapsed, according to the BBC, PBS and AP. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack unprecedented and said it followed weeks of efforts to wear down Russian air defenses. Overnight, Ukraine also targeted refineries in Russia's Krasnodar region, Deutsche Welle reported.
stories.why_it_matters: The bridge is a main route for Russian military and civilian supplies into Crimea, so its loss could affect the front line and Russia's hold on the peninsula. The strike came a day before Vladimir Putin was due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, where Ukraine's future may be discussed.
stories.background: Russia seized and annexed Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 and opened the 19-kilometre road and rail bridge across the Kerch Strait in 2018. It is the only fixed link between Russia and the peninsula, and Putin has treated it as a symbol of the annexation. Ukraine has attacked it several times since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, including truck-bomb and sea-drone attacks in 2022 and 2023. Destroying it has long been a stated goal for Kyiv.

facts.text: Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge with drones and missiles, and one span partly collapsed.
Ukraine says the attack took weeks to plan, and Zelenskyy described a weeks-long effort to wear down Russian air defenses before the strike.
The bridge is the only structure connecting Russia to occupied Crimea and a key route for military and civilian supplies to Russian troops.
Ukraine also targeted two industrial facilities in Russia's Krasnodar region overnight, reportedly refineries.
The attack came ahead of a three-way meeting of Putin, Trump and Xi in Shenzhen, China.

stories.headline: Trump arrives in China for APEC ahead of first three-way meeting with Xi and Putin
stories.summary: President Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping greeted him on the tarmac. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are due to hold three-way talks on Thursday. Xi met Putin separately on Wednesday and called for closer political and military ties between China and Russia.
stories.why_it_matters: A meeting of the US, Chinese and Russian leaders could shape the course of the war in Ukraine, the US war with Iran and trade between the world's largest economies, all of which affect prices and security. The talks come as US intelligence assesses that Putin will keep fighting in Ukraine, according to The New York Times.
stories.background: APEC is a yearly forum of 21 Pacific Rim economies, and China is hosting it this year in Shenzhen. A Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was first floated by the Kremlin in September after a Putin-Trump phone call, and China later confirmed it. Trump came to China after stops in Southeast Asia, including an ASEAN summit and a visit to Manila. Xi visited Washington in September, and Trump greeted him on the tarmac then.

facts.text: Xi personally greeted Trump on the tarmac after Air Force One landed in Shenzhen, returning a gesture Trump made during Xi's September visit to Washington.
The three-way meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin is scheduled for Thursday.
The Kremlin said Putin and Trump would meet several times during the summit, though no formal bilateral session had been scheduled.
Xi urged closer political and military ties with Russia when he met Putin on Wednesday.

The New York Times reported that US intelligence believes Putin will continue the Ukraine war despite the talks, and that Trump has halted some sanctions on Russia and announced US purchases of Russian diesel.
CBS reported Trump may also meet North Korea's Kim Jong Un.
In a speech, Putin said Europe was in a "humiliating decline", The Guardian reported.

stories.headline: Iran fires on Kuwait and Bahrain after US strikes Iranian island
stories.summary: US fighter jets struck an Iranian Revolutionary Guard missile launch site on Qeshm Island on Tuesday in what US officials called self-defense, after Iran fired drones at a US radar site in Bahrain for the third time in five days. Iran then fired at a US air base in Kuwait and at targets in Bahrain, and both countries said they repelled the attacks. Iran's army chief warned of a "more devastating" response to any new attacks, France 24 reported.
stories.why_it_matters: The exchanges end a roughly two-month lull in Iranian attacks on Gulf states and threaten shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil and gas that affects fuel prices worldwide. US troops based in Kuwait and Bahrain are in the line of fire.
stories.background: The US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in late February, starting a war that has spilled into neighboring Gulf states hosting US forces. Iran has repeatedly targeted US bases and shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, and the US has struck Iranian sites in response. Bahrain hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, and Kuwait hosts several US bases. Qatar has acted as a mediator.

Bahrain and Kuwait said they repelled air attacks on Wednesday, and Gulf countries said some missiles and drones came from Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen.
The Wall Street Journal reported Iran had set a natural gas tanker on fire in the Strait of Hormuz before the latest attacks.

stories.headline: Five EU countries plan deportation hub in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers
stories.summary: Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece announced plans in Vienna on Monday to set up a "return hub" in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe. stories.background: European governments have been under political pressure to deport more people whose asylum claims are rejected. Britain tried a similar Rwanda scheme from 2022 but its courts blocked it and the next government scrapped it in 2024. In September, the five EU countries agreed on a shared model for return hubs outside the EU. Rwanda has presented itself as a willing partner, while rights groups cite reports of abuses there.

stories.summary: Britain imposed sanctions on Israeli construction companies building settlements in the occupied West Bank, with The Times of Israel counting eight firms. stories.headline: Isolated Awá group emerges from Brazil's Amazon, raising fears over invasions
stories.summary: About 20 members of the isolated Awá people emerged from the forest in Brazil's Amazon and made contact with villagers, several organizations reported Tuesday. They appeared thin and hungry and accepted food to take back to their territory, according to reports. Brazil's government policy is to avoid contact with isolated groups unless their survival is at risk.

stories.headline: Nvidia beats forecasts in first report since Huang's exit; board says he won't return
stories.summary: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue roughly double a year earlier and raised its outlook, in its first results under interim chief executive Colette Kress. Its board chair said the company does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned last week and had sought to return. Tech stocks and U.S. stock futures rose on Wednesday as the results eased worries about AI spending.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the index funds held in many 401(k)s, so its results helped stop a multi-day slide in tech stocks that had cut into retirement balances.
stories.background: Nvidia makes the chips used to train and run most artificial intelligence systems, and enthusiasm for AI has driven much of the stock market's gains since 2023. Co-founder Jensen Huang, its only chief executive until now, resigned on Nov. 12 after reports linked him to a former executive of a Singapore customer whom U.S. officials suspect of spying for China. The board made finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO and named Harvey Jones chair. Nvidia's shares had their worst week in 19 months before the report, and a wider sell-off in tech stocks ran for several days.

Nvidia did not file its usual quarterly 10-Q report with the SEC alongside its results; MarketWatch said this suggested Huang's resignation involved more than personal conduct.

stories.summary: St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said the Federal Reserve will likely need several interest-rate increases, possibly four, by spring to bring inflation down. Inflation picked up this year as the war with Iran pushed energy prices higher, and consumer prices were up about 3.7% from a year earlier in September. The Fed's key rate is about 3.9%, and its next meeting is in December, where traders expect an increase. Musalem heads one of the 12 regional Fed banks and is known as one of the officials most focused on fighting inflation.

stories.summary: The Treasury Department issued final rules for a 2022 law that requires most new 401(k) and 403(b) plans to sign workers up automatically. Reuters noted the rules came years after the law passed.
stories.why_it_matters: Workers at many employers that started retirement plans since late 2022 will be enrolled automatically and have to opt out if they don't want to save.
stories.background: The SECURE 2.0 Act, passed by Congress in December 2022, requires most 401(k) and 403(b) plans created after that date to enroll eligible workers automatically. Studies have long shown that people save more when they must opt out rather than opt in. Treasury and the IRS proposed rules in January 2025, and the White House finished reviewing the final version in October. The requirement took effect for plan years starting in 2025, and employers have been following a good-faith reading of the law while waiting for the rules.

facts.text: Treasury issued final rules for automatic enrollment in retirement plans, Reuters and Fox Business reported.

Under the law, covered plans must enroll workers at a default rate of 3% to 10% of pay, rising by 1 percentage point a year to at least 10% and no more than 15%; workers can opt out or choose a different rate, according to the IRS.
Small businesses with 10 or fewer employees, companies in business for less than three years, church plans and government plans are exempt, according to the IRS.
The White House regulatory office finished its review of the final rules on Oct. 16, a retirement-plan trade group reported.

framing.note: Emphasizes the possible boost to retirement savings.

stories.headline: City halts work at sites tied to contractors in fatal Flatbush collapse
stories.summary: After an apartment building in Flatbush collapsed into a neighboring construction site and killed eight people, city inspectors have fanned out to about 160 sites where the same contractors work, and some of those jobs have been stopped. A tenant of the collapsed building says in a new lawsuit that he warned his landlord about cracks weeks earlier. The cause has not been determined.
stories.why_it_matters: The sweep could pause construction near many New Yorkers' homes, and the outcome may shape how the city and Albany police work next to older buildings. So far the follow-up reporting in the digest comes from left-leaning and center outlets only.
stories.background: On Nov. 11-12 a nearly century-old, three-story apartment building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a construction site next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue. Eight people died, including two children, and more than a dozen were hurt. Earlier this year the Department of Buildings had halted demolition at the neighboring site over inadequate protection for adjoining buildings, then lifted the order in May. Mayor Zohran Mamdani ordered an emergency review of other sites linked to the companies involved, and Gov. Kathy Hochul faces renewed debate over the state's Scaffold Law, which governs construction-injury liability.

facts.text: The collapse killed eight people, two children and six adults.
Mayor Mamdani said building inspectors launched an emergency review of about 160 locations citywide where contractors from the collapse site have been working.

A Gothamist analysis found the Department of Buildings is targeting five projects linked to engineers involved in the construction next to the collapsed building, and inspections have halted work at some sites.
Tenant Dengane Omari Jack says in a lawsuit that he sent his landlord photos of damage around the building's entrance weeks before the collapse.
The Department of Buildings had ordered demolition stopped at the adjacent site in March over inadequate overhead protection for neighbors, and lifted the order in May.
Officials have not said what caused the collapse; reports say it is unclear whether demolition or later excavation played a role.
City & State reported that Gov. Hochul did not rule out changes to the state Scaffold Law after the collapse.

stories.headline: NYC public school enrollment falls by about 23,000 students
stories.summary: Preliminary Education Department figures released Monday show city public schools lost about 23,000 students, nearly 3%, from last year. Officials expect further declines, which raises questions about school budgets and possible closures.
stories.why_it_matters: Fewer students can mean smaller school budgets, merged programs or closures, which affects families choosing schools and the city's spending.
stories.background: New York City runs the country's largest school system. Enrollment has been falling for years, with the city losing about 200,000 students over the past decade, a trend seen in districts nationwide as birth rates fall and families choose charter or private schools or leave the city. Since the pandemic the city has largely kept school budgets steady despite the losses. Mayor Mamdani's schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, now faces decisions on how to adjust.

stories.headline: MTA aims to modernize signals across the entire subway by 2050
stories.summary: MTA Chair Janno Lieber announced a plan to install modern signals throughout the subway system by 2050. Only Gothamist covered the announcement in the digest.
stories.why_it_matters: Old signals are a major cause of subway delays; modern ones let trains run closer together and more reliably, but riders would see the full benefit only over decades.
stories.background: Much of the subway still runs on signals dating to the 1930s. Newer communications-based train control (CBTC) systems, already on lines such as the L and 7, let trains run more frequently. The MTA's 2025-2029 capital plan funds signal work on dozens of miles of track, but an MTA consultant has reported that every current signal upgrade is behind schedule.

concept.explanation: The Federal Open Market Committee is the group of Federal Reserve officials who vote on interest rates about eight times a year. Three weeks after each meeting, the Fed publishes the minutes: a detailed summary of what officials argued about, including how many worried about inflation versus unemployment. Investors read them for hints about the next rate decision, because a hint of higher rates can push up Treasury yields within minutes. Those yields feed into the rates on mortgages, car loans and credit cards, so the minutes can nudge what you pay to borrow even though nothing is decided in them.
